title: GoDaddy Says AI-Driven Cyberattack Exposed Website Customer Information
content:
(VINnews) – GoDaddy said an AI-driven cyberattack exposed profile, settings and contact information associated with its Websites + Marketing product, though the company said the attacker did not obtain passwords or access customer accounts.

The incident occurred Sept. 18 and was detected the following day, according to a notice sent to customers. The attacker obtained information through an application programming interface, or API, including contact details customers had supplied for publication on their websites.
GoDaddy said its investigation found that the attacker’s activity was limited to reading the exposed information. The company said there was no evidence that the attacker changed websites, accessed accounts or took other actions affecting customer products.
The company described the incident as its first known AI-driven cyberattack. It said it responded immediately, engaged cybersecurity experts and worked with industry partners to stop the activity.
GoDaddy also reported the incident to law enforcement and voluntarily notified the Federal Trade Commission and data protection authorities in the United Kingdom and European Union.
The company said the incident had been contained and that it had taken additional steps to defend against similar attacks.
GoDaddy urged customers to remain alert for suspicious emails and phone calls, warning that exposed contact information could be used in phishing attempts. The company recommended enabling two-step verification, which adds an extra layer of security to accounts.
GoDaddy said it would never request passwords, payment details or verification codes by email, text message or phone.

report.summary: GoDaddy says an AI-driven API attack in September exposed website profile and contact data for Websites + Marketing customers, without compromising passwords or accounts.
report.background: GoDaddy has become one of the most repeatedly targeted companies in web infrastructure: a 2021 breach hit WordPress hosting, and the company disclosed in 2022 that an intruder had accessed data for about 1.2 million customers over multiple years. Hosting and registrar providers are attractive because a single credential or API flaw can unlock millions of small-business sites. What is new here is the stated cause. Security researchers have spent the past two years demonstrating that large language models and autonomous agents can automate reconnaissance, fuzz APIs, chain small logic flaws and adapt in real time — compressing attack timelines from weeks to hours. Regulators have noticed: the FTC has been actively scrutinizing data-handling at large platforms, and GDPR rules require EU/UK breach notification. GoDaddy's voluntary disclosure to the FTC and European regulators signals that AI-automated intrusion is now being treated as a distinct, reportable category of incident rather than ordinary hacking.
key_points: An API was the entry point. Attackers reached customer profile, settings and website contact details through an application programming interface, the machine-to-machine channel that powers modern web products and is often less carefully guarded than a login page. GoDaddy says the activity was read-only: no passwords taken, no accounts accessed, no websites altered.

The timeline was tight. Intrusion occurred on Sept. 18 and was detected the next day, after which GoDaddy says it engaged outside security experts, worked with industry partners to stop the activity and contained it. The company has not published technical indicators describing what the AI actually did.

GoDaddy calls it a first. The company described the event as its first known AI-driven cyberattack, a notable claim from an organization with a long history of breaches. It has not explained whether AI handled reconnaissance, exploitation or evasion, leaving the assertion hard to independently verify.

Regulators were notified. GoDaddy reported to law enforcement and voluntarily alerted the US Federal Trade Commission plus data protection authorities in the UK and EU, a move that raises the compliance stakes for how AI-enabled intrusions get disclosed.

Customers face phishing risk. Although no credentials leaked, the exposed contact information is exactly what convincing business-email-compromise and voice-phishing campaigns need. GoDaddy urged two-step verification and reminded users it never asks for passwords, payment details or verification codes.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this is a marker: autonomous or LLM-assisted intrusion has moved from conference demos to a named cause in a public breach disclosure. Security vendors will accelerate investment in AI-driven offense simulation and API-specific defenses, and insurers and auditors will start asking pointed questions about agentic tooling in the threat model. For developers, the lesson is that APIs, not login forms, are the soft underbelly — rate limiting, schema validation, least-privilege tokens and anomaly detection on read patterns matter more than ever. For regular users, the practical fallout is phishing: expect tailored emails and calls citing real business details. Nothing changes about passwords here, but two-factor authentication and skepticism toward unsolicited contact are now baseline hygiene.
report.tools: Worth watching: OWASP API Security Top 10 and OWASP ZAP for API testing fundamentals; Burp Suite for hands-on probing; NVIDIA Garak and Microsoft PyRIT for probing LLM and agent behavior; MITRE ATLAS as the ATT&CK-style knowledge base for AI-enabled attacks; promptfoo for red-teaming prompts. On the defense side, commercial API security platforms (Salt Security, Noname, Traceable) specialize in detecting abnormal read patterns. For individual users, enabling two-step verification on GoDaddy and other accounts is the immediate action.
